parts.partTitle: How JVM Memory Distinguishes Classes from Objects

beats.headline: Does new copy your class bytecode every time?
beats.subline: Allocating a thousand objects does not duplicate method code in memory.
beats.narration: When you instantiate a class a thousand times, does the JVM duplicate your method bytecode a thousand times on the Heap? Let us trace how HotSpot splits class metadata from instance state.

beats.title: HotSpot JVM Memory Layout
beats.subtitle: Native Metaspace vs Garbage-Collected Heap

nodes.label: BankAccount.java
nodes.detail: Source compiled by javac into class bytecode

nodes.label: Metaspace (Native)
nodes.detail: Stores method bytecode, symbols & vtables once

nodes.label: Heap Instances
nodes.detail: Independent memory blocks for alice & bob fields

beats.narration: HotSpot loads class bytecode into native Metaspace, storing method tables exactly once. The JVM then creates a class mirror on the Heap, while every new call allocates fresh heap memory for instance fields.

beats.title: Metaspace Blueprint vs Heap Allocation

top.label: Metaspace (Class Level)

bottom.label: Heap (Instance Level)
bottom.code:
BankAccount alice = new BankAccount("ACC-101", 50_000);
BankAccount bob = new BankAccount("ACC-202", 12_000);

beats.narration: Class definitions reside in native Metaspace. Calling new allocates a distinct memory block on the Java Heap, holding only its own field state while sharing the underlying bytecode.

beats.title: Default Initialization vs Local Variables

steps.explanation: Automatically zero-initialized during object allocation (null, 0, false).
No default values! Reading uninitialized locals causes compile-time errors.

beats.narration: Instance fields get automatic default values like null, false, or zero when allocated. But local variables inside methods receive no defaults at all, making uninitialized reads a strict compile time error.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Class metadata resides once in Metaspace
Heap instances store individual field state
Instance fields auto-initialize; locals do not

beats.headline: Why does adding one constructor break your callers?
beats.subline: The silent default constructor vanishes the moment you declare a custom constructor.
beats.narration: You write a parameterized constructor to enforce validation, and suddenly callers using the default constructor fail to compile. Here is the strict compiler rule governing Java constructors.

beats.title: The Vanishing Default Constructor

steps.explanation: Declaring any constructor stops javac from synthesizing public Product().
Callers expecting a no-args constructor now fail to compile.

beats.narration: When a class defines zero constructors, javac synthesizes a default parameterless constructor. But the exact instant you declare any parameterized constructor, that automatic default constructor disappears completely.

beats.title: Telescoping vs Builder Pattern

top.label: Telescoping Constructors
points: Consecutive int parameters lead to call site bugs
Requires checking signature to understand flags

beats.narration: Passing consecutive integer arguments into overloaded constructors leads to subtle parameter order bugs. A static inner Builder makes optional configuration self-documenting, explicit, and safe.

beats.title: The Silent Void Constructor Trap

steps.explanation: Adding void turns a constructor into a normal instance method.
javac generates default constructor; title is left as null.

beats.narration: If you accidentally add void to a constructor signature, Java treats it as a standard instance method. The compiler still synthesizes a default constructor, leaving your object fields completely uninitialized.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Never put return types like void on constructors
Use Builders for complex optional arguments

beats.narration: That is constructor design done right. In Part 3, we reveal why leaking this inside a constructor can expose uninitialized final fields to concurrent threads.

parts.partTitle: The `this` Keyword & The Deadly `this` Escape Bug

beats.headline: Leaking this in a constructor bypasses final guarantees!
beats.subline: Concurrent threads can read null from a final field before construction finishes.
beats.narration: You marked a field final so it could never be null. But passing this to an event listener inside your constructor creates a race condition that exposes null anyway.

beats.title: Field Shadowing & Constructor Chaining

steps.explanation: Delegates to canonical constructor. Must be the first statement.
Disambiguates parameter host from instance field this.host.

beats.narration: Use this dot to disambiguate parameters that shadow instance fields. To chain constructors, call this with arguments as your very first statement to centralize field assignment logic.

beats.title: The Hazardous this Escape Bug

top.label: Constructor Listener Registration
points: Event bus thread invokes methods immediately
Reads final field as null before assignment

bottom.label: Safe Static Factory Pattern
points: Guarantees memory visibility for final fields

beats.narration: Registering an object with an event bus inside its constructor allows external threads to invoke methods on a partially constructed object. Always separate object initialization from listener registration.

beats.title: Safe Publication with Static Factories

steps.explanation: Ensures all final fields are initialized before external access.
Publishes fully constructed object safely to external listeners.

beats.narration: Instead of registering inside the constructor, complete object construction first. Use a static factory method to instantiate the object cleanly before handing its reference to external services.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: this(...) must execute first in constructor chaining
Never pass this to listeners during construction

beats.headline: Which initializer block executes first when an object is born?
beats.subline: Static blocks, super constructors, and instance initializers follow a strict sequence.
beats.narration: If a class contains static blocks, instance fields, and a constructor, in what exact order does the JVM execute them? Let us trace object creation step by step.

beats.title: Object Initialization Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Deterministic sequence defined by Java Language Spec

nodes.label: 1. Static Initializers
nodes.detail: Runs once when class is loaded into JVM

nodes.label: 2. Super Constructor
nodes.detail: Parent class constructor completes via super()

nodes.label: 4. Constructor Body
nodes.detail: Custom validation & field assignment executes last

beats.narration: Static blocks execute once when the class initializes. When calling new, the JVM completes the superclass constructor first, runs instance field initializers next, and finally executes your constructor body.

beats.title: Method Overload Resolution Ladder
beats.subtitle: How javac picks the matching signature

nodes.label: Step 2: Widening
nodes.detail: Primitive widening like int to long or double

nodes.label: Step 3: Autoboxing
nodes.detail: Box primitive to wrapper like int to Integer

beats.narration: When resolving overloaded methods, javac evaluates signatures in four strict stages: exact match first, followed by primitive widening, autoboxing, and finally varargs fallbacks.

beats.title: Primitive Widening vs Autoboxing

steps.explanation: Primitive widening (int to long) takes priority over autoboxing (int to Integer).
Autoboxing and varargs are evaluated only if no widened overload matches.

beats.narration: Calling log with integer five matches log long before log Integer. Primitive widening beats autoboxing because widening was introduced in Java 1.0, preserving backward compatibility.

takeaways: Static initializers run once per class loading
Instance fields initialize before constructor body
Primitive widening beats autoboxing in overload resolution
